units.text: Anastatus disparis Ruschka (Hymenoptera: Eupelmidae) has been recorded as an important egg endoparasitoid of Lymantria dispar L. (Lepidoptera: Erebidae) (Alalouni et al. 2013, Avci 2009, Crossman 1925, Kurir 1944, Liu et al. 2017) and is widely distributed in Europe and Asia (Yan et al. 1989). In addition, as a potential biological control agent of L. dispar, A. disparis was imported to North America in the early 1900s (Crossman 1925, Yan et al. 1989). Field investigation reveals that, together with Ooencyrtus kuvanae (Howard) (Hymenoptera: Encrytidae), which is also the main egg parasitoid of L. dispar, their parasitism rates may reach 20–40% (Brown 1984, Brown and Cameron 1982, Hoy 1976, Reardon 1981). Beyond L. dispar, multiple lepidopteran forest pests—such as Malacosoma neustria (Malane), Odonestis pruni L., Antheraea pernyi Guénerin-Méneville, Dendrolimus punctatus tabulaeformis (Walker), Lycorma delicatula (Walker), and Actias selene ningpoana Felder—can be parasitized (Li and Lou 1992, Li et al. 2001, Yan et al. 1989). Besides Lymantria dispar, great efforts have been made to mass rear Anastatus disparis to control Dictyoploca japonica Moore in China, with the eggs of Antheraea pernyi serving as suitable factitious hosts (Yan et al. 1989). Adult females can lay hundreds of eggs over their lifetime and live approximately 1 mo in the wild, whereas males live approximately 1 wk (Liu et al. 2015, Yan et al. 1989). Successful reproduction of wasps is important for population succession and control of host pests in the wild. Here, we tested the role of age in terms of reproductive success including the parasitism ratio, eclosion ratio, and sex ratio in Anastatus disparis. Alternatively, similar to many long-lived species, reproductive performances increase with age in early life, stabilize at mid-age, and decline in old age (Clutton-Brock 1988, Forslund and Pärt 1995, Newton 1989). Additionally, because of low-quality phenotypes (Marshall et al. 2010, Rasekh et al. 2022, Tovar et al. 2025, Włodarczyk and Minias 2020), our results may show decreasing reproductive success with female age. Egg size is thought to be an important component of quality phenotypes (Bernardo 1996), and egg quality and size laid by females of different ages were also assessed in A. disparis. In either case, we expected to see a difference in reproductive performance between young females and old females.

Parasitoids. An Anastatus disparis colony was established from a population reared on egg masses of L. dispar collected in Longhua County, Hebei Province $( \mathsf { N } 4 1 ^ { \circ } 3 1 ^ { \prime } , \mathsf { E } 1 1 7 ^ { \circ } 7 4 ^ { \prime } )$ in March 2012 and then subsequently maintained on eggs of Antheraea pernyi for approximately 140 to 145 generations. The development time from eggs to adults was found to be 19–22 d for males and 20–28 d for females reared at $2 6 – 2 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } ,$ and the entire development was completed inside the host (Liu et al. 2015). Both females and males can immediately mate after eclosion, and males engage in extreme fights to acquire mating opportunities (Liu and Hao 2019). Therefore, before wasp eclosion, the parasitized hosts were isolated individually in polyethene tubes (height 7.5 cm; diameter 1 cm) to prevent mating among wasps and male injury during fighting before the start of the experiment. The peak eclosion period was between 9:00 a.m. and 12:00 noon, and all experimental wasps were collected during this period. To obtain mated females for our experiment, newly emerged males were supplied to a virgin female (1 d old) for mating, and mating behavior was observed. All female adults were fed honey water (4:6) until the start of the experiment (Yan et al. 1989).

Yan et al. 1989) were set up. Before beginning the experiment, each tested female was isolated and reared in a cylindrical rearing box (5 cm high, 5-cm diameter). Thus, the wasps used in the experiment were naive, without ovipositing experience, and kept for 2, 15, and 30 d, respectively, before the experiment began. Generally, oviposition experiments for each female were conducted for 4 h ranging from 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., and the entire process was video recorded. On the basis of a review of the video, both the latency period before oviposition and the period of oviposition were determined. Parasitoid wasps can attack one host egg multiple times, which may result in some unsuccessful oviposition. In Anastatus disparis, a bout of oviposition was thought to be completed when the individual parasitized a new host or was physically away from the previously parasitized host for at least 1 min (Liu et al. 2018). In total, 16–20 replicates were performed for each treatment. After 4 h, all hosts and 1 female were removed from the Petri dish. Hosts (i.e., eight) from two replicate experiments for each treatment were immediately dissected using forceps under a microscope (Leica M205A, Germany). The wasp egg of A. disparis is long and elliptical, and the long-axis diameter was measured by digital microscopy system (Keyens VHX-5000, Japan) as the egg size. The remaining host eggs in a dish were isolated individually by number in polyethene tubes mentioned above, sealed with cotton wool, and incubated at $28^{\circ}C \pm 0.5^{\circ}C,70\% \pm 5\%$ relative humidity, and a photoperiod of 14 h light:10 h dark until adults emerged. All hosts were incubated for 60 d to ensure that the developing parasitoids had the opportunity to undergo full development from egg to larva to pupa in the host and finally emerge as adults (Liu et al. 2015). Then, we dissected any remaining host eggs and recorded the number of dead larvae, pupae, or adult wasps that had failed to complete development using forceps under a microscope (Leica M205A). In each dish, successful oviposition, latency to oviposition, and oviposition duration were recorded by watching videos associated with the above results of adult eclosion. Host eggs were dissected from unmated Antheraea pernyi females, a method that may inadvertently influence offspring sex ratio because of host quality variation (Liu et al. 2017). To isolate the effects of female age on reproductive success, we intentionally excluded sex ratio measurements to avoid confounding factors related to host manipulation.

Statistical analysis. All analyses were performed with R 3.6.1 software (R Core Team 2019). A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with the multcomp package was applied to analyze the effects of female status and age on outcomes of offspring successfully produced and eclosion, offspring number produced/emerged per female, period of oviposition, and egg size. In each model, female status and age were fixed effects, and female identification was considered a random effect for control differences between females. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) was used to check the goodness of fit. Therefore, the model with a low AIC value was regarded as a suitable model. GLMM logistic regression using binomial distribution and logit link function was applied to analyze the data on outcomes of offspring successfully produced and eclosion. A Poisson distribution model and log link function were used for count data of offspring number. Data on the period of oviposition and egg size were analyzed using a GLMM with a normal error structure (and log transformation to normalize the residuals if necessary). In addition, quasibinomial and quasi-Poisson regressions were used to correct for data overdispersion (i.e., the ratio of residual deviance and residual df . 1), and significance was assessed by the F statistic (Crawley 2007).

Effects of female status and age. During the experimental period of 4 h, 64.4% of females (67/104) successfully laid eggs into a host, producing 258 offspring wasps $( 2 . 4 8 \pm 0 . 1 9$ offspring wasps per female). Female mating status and age had no effect on the probability of females successfully laying eggs (Table 1; female status: $\chi ^ { 2 } = 0 . \dot { 7 } 1$ ; P ¼ 0.532; age: $\chi ^ { 2 } = 3 . 1 4 3 ;$ P ¼ 0.226) or the number of offspring produced per female (Fig. 1a, female status: $F = 0 . 7 3 2$ ; degrees of freedom [df] ¼ 1,102; P ¼ 0.451; age: F ¼ 1.86; df ¼ 2,101; P ¼ 0.337).
